entities.summary:
The House of Romanov, Russia's ruling dynasty from Michael Romanov's election by the Zemsky Sobor (1613) following the Time of Troubles (a succession crisis) until Nicholas II's abdication (1917) and execution (1918), ruled Russia for 304 years through its transformation from a backward Muscovite principality into a European great power and the world's largest territorial state. The Romanovs' reign encompasses Russia's European emergence under Peter the Great, Catherine the Great's Enlightenment absolutism, the Napoleonic Wars, the emancipation of serfs (1861), and the 1917 Revolution that ended the dynasty.

Key Romanov reigns: Peter the Great (r. 1682-1725) Westernized Russia, built St. Petersburg (on land conquered from Sweden), established the Russian Navy, and personally led military campaigns — transforming Russia into a Baltic power; Catherine the Great (r. 1762-1796) — actually a German princess (Sophia of Anhalt-Zerbst) who had her husband Peter III murdered/deposed — expanded Russia's borders to the Black Sea, partitioned Poland three times, and maintained correspondence with Voltaire and Diderot while suppressing the Pugachev Rebellion.

The dynasty's end: Nicholas II's disastrous military leadership in WWI (1914-1917), combined with food shortages, military mutinies, and the Rasputin scandal, led to the February Revolution (1917); Nicholas abdicated March 1917. The Bolsheviks executed Nicholas, his wife Alexandra, and their five children (including Anastasia) at Yekaterinburg on July 17, 1918 — one of history's most consequential royal executions, inaugurating Soviet Russia. Romanov descendants (via Nicholas II's siblings) survive today as claimants to a restored Russian throne.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The House of Romanov — ruling Russia's transformation from feudal principality to world superpower across 304 years, ending in the Bolshevik execution that inaugurated Soviet Russia — is one of history's most consequential dynasties, and its collapse is one of the defining moments of 20th-century history.
